name: Arron Kian Parejas
stories:
On October 19–20, 2025, I stood alongside four fellow students from the School of Computing of Holy Angel University as we competed in the SkyDev Hack Play and Learn Hackathon. What started as an intense two-day challenge quickly became one of the most meaningful experiences of my journey as a developer.

Our project, Lumo, was born from empathy. Inside our university—specifically the SJH Building—I had repeatedly seen a visually impaired professor navigating daily obstacles that most of us never think twice about. Those moments stayed with me. I kept asking myself: If we have AI, computer vision, and smartphones in our pockets, why can’t we use them to give independence back to someone who needs it most?

That question became the foundation of Lumo. I proposed the idea of combining AI-driven object detection with real-time voice guidance to help visually impaired individuals navigate safely and independently. After brainstorming as a team, we unanimously chose Lumo—because it wasn’t just technically challenging, it mattered.

I took responsibility for the AI models, backend logic, and cloud integration, while my teammates—Francoise Gurango, Graciella Jimenez, Kalel Marquez, and Prince Laxamana—focused on crafting an intuitive, accessible UI/UX. Within the first hour, we already had a working design direction. From there, it was a race against time.

The first night pushed me to my limits. I stayed up refining the backend and AI pipeline until around 4:30 a.m., ensuring the system could work offline with high accuracy. Exhaustion was real—but giving up was never an option. On the second day, just 30 minutes before submission, disaster struck: our Google Maps integration failed during Docker deployment. In that moment, everything we worked for was on the line. I dropped everything, isolated the issue, and fixed it just in time. When the app finally ran, the relief was indescribable.

During the final presentation, I confidently defended Lumo in front of industry professionals—explaining not just how it worked, but why it needed to exist. I spoke about scalability, feasibility, and impact, but more importantly, I spoke about people. About dignity. About independence.

When Holy Angel University was announced as Champion, it felt surreal. The judges recognized Lumo for its technical excellence, creativity, and social relevance—but for me, the real victory was knowing we built something with purpose.

I’m deeply grateful to our coaches, Professor Ulysses Raymond Monsale and Mr. Tjakoen Stolk, whose mentorship and guidance shaped our approach and mindset throughout the competition. I’m also thankful to the School of Computing administration for continuously fostering an environment where innovation and compassion can thrive.

Above all, I thank the Lord—for the strength to push through exhaustion, the clarity to solve problems under pressure, and the wisdom to use technology for something greater than myself.

This experience reaffirmed what I believe as a developer: technology becomes truly powerful when guided by empathy and purpose. Lumo wasn’t just a hackathon project—it was proof that when we listen, observe, and care, we can build solutions that genuinely change lives.

And this is only the beginning.

name: Jansen C. Cruz
stories:
Impact, to me, has never been about recognition—it has always been about usefulness. One of the most meaningful projects I’ve worked on was developing an Electronic Medical Records (EMR) system in collaboration with the College of Nursing. It started with a simple but urgent problem: healthcare staff at Brgy. Ninoy Aquino were managing patient records manually, and files were often disorganized or at risk of being lost.

We saw the gap clearly. Records weren’t just documents—they represented real people, real health histories, and real decisions. So our team built a system that centralized and digitized their data, improving workflow efficiency and record management. When the system was finally deployed and actively used by the healthcare workers, I realized something powerful: technology becomes meaningful when it directly supports people on the ground. Knowing that something I helped build contributes to community healthcare is incredibly fulfilling.

But growth doesn’t come without pressure. During the GDG HAU competition, just hours before submission, our machine learning model still wasn’t producing reliable results. Tension filled the room. Deadlines were closing in, and frustration was building. Instead of panicking, we made a difficult but important decision—we paused. We stepped away briefly, took a short walk, and cleared our minds.

When we came back, everything changed. We simplified the pipeline, reviewed each component step-by-step, and traced the issue to incorrect preprocessing that was corrupting the model’s inputs. By focusing on fundamentals instead of overengineering the solution, we stabilized the model just in time. That experience taught me a lesson I carry with me today: clarity under pressure is more powerful than panic.

Another defining lesson came from an unfinished project earlier in my journey. At the time, I was obsessed with making the system technically impressive. I added advanced features and experimented with complex implementations—but I forgot who I was building for. The project stalled because the foundation wasn’t simple or practical enough.

That failure reshaped my mindset. I learned that great technology isn’t about complexity—it’s about solving the right problem in the simplest, most effective way. Since then, I begin every project by clearly defining the core problem and building the simplest solution that works before improving it.

My journey as a developer truly became serious in 2022 during my senior high school years. Although I had been curious about coding since I was 12, that was the moment I made a commitment: to study and build something every single day, 365 days a year. I didn’t rely on motivation—I relied on discipline.

I documented everything. What began as a single folder in 2022 slowly grew month by month. Now, years later, those folders stack on top of each other—visible proof of growth, failures, experiments, and progress. Whenever I feel stuck, I look back at that archive and remind myself how far consistency can take you.

More than talent, I believe excellence is built through sustained effort. Discipline shaped my mindset. Pressure strengthened my problem-solving. Failure refined my perspective. And real-world impact gave my work purpose.

If I am considered for recognition, it would not simply represent achievement—it would represent the values I stand for: building solutions that matter, growing consistently, and using technology to create real impact. And for me, this journey of learning, building, and improving is only just beginning.
